UPSTREAM: build_bug.h: remove most of dummy BUILD_BUG_ON stubs for Sparse The introduction of these dummy BUILD_BUG_ON stubs dates back to commmit 903c0c7cdc21 ("sparse: define dummy BUILD_BUG_ON definition for sparse"). At that time, BUILD_BUG_ON() was implemented with the negative array trick *and* the link-time trick, like this: extern int __build_bug_on_failed; #define BUILD_BUG_ON(condition) \ do { \ ((void)sizeof(char[1 - 2*!!(condition)])); \ if (condition) __build_bug_on_failed = 1; \ } while(0) Sparse is more strict about the negative array trick than GCC because Sparse requires the array length to be really constant. Here is the simple test code for the macro above: static const int x = 0; BUILD_BUG_ON(x); GCC is absolutely fine with it (-Wvla was enabled only very recently), but Sparse warns like this: error: bad constant expression error: cannot size expression (If you are using a newer version of Sparse, you will see a different warning message, "warning: Variable length array is used".) Anyway, Sparse was producing many false positives, and noisier than it should be at that time. With the previous commit, the leftover negative array trick is gone. Sparse is fine with the current BUILD_BUG_ON(), which is implemented by using the 'error' attribute. I am keeping the stub for BUILD_BUG_ON_ZERO(). Otherwise, Sparse would complain about the following code, which GCC is fine with: static const int x = 0; int y = BUILD_BUG_ON_ZERO(x); BUG=b:124400293 TEST=None Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/1542856462-18836-3-git-send-email-yamada.masahiro@socionext.com Signed-off-by: Masahiro Yamada <yamada.masahiro@socionext.com> Acked-by: Kees Cook <keescook@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Luc Van Oostenryck <luc.vanoostenryck@gmail.com> Reviewed-by: Nick Desaulniers <ndesaulniers@google.com> Tested-by: Nick Desaulniers <ndesaulniers@google.com> Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org> Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org> (cherry picked from commit 527edbc18a70e745740ef31edb0ffefb2f161afa) Signed-off-by: Yan-Hsuan Chuang <yhchuang@realtek.com> Change-Id: Ia7d84098d5cdcc21df5f123cfba55d31b6f62f22 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/1732990 Tested-by: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Commit-Ready: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Legacy-Commit-Queue: Commit Bot <commit-bot@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Brian Norris <briannorris@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Sean Paul <seanpaul@chromium.org>

UPSTREAM: build_bug.h: add wrapper for _Static_assert BUILD_BUG_ON() is a little annoying, since it cannot be used outside function scope. So one cannot put assertions about the sizeof() a struct next to the struct definition, but has to hide that in some more or less arbitrary function. Since gcc 4.6 (which is now also the required minimum), there is support for the C11 _Static_assert in all C modes, including gnu89. So add a simple wrapper for that. _Static_assert() requires a message argument, which is usually quite redundant (and I believe that bug got fixed at least in newer C++ standards), but we can easily work around that with a little macro magic, making it optional. For example, adding static_assert(sizeof(struct printf_spec) == 8); in vsprintf.c and modifying that struct to violate it, one gets ./include/linux/build_bug.h:78:41: error: static assertion failed: "sizeof(struct printf_spec) == 8" #define __static_assert(expr, msg, ...) _Static_assert(expr, "" msg "") godbolt.org suggests that _Static_assert() has been support by clang since at least 3.0.0. biod: Mitigate race between powerbutton and fingerprint events. Currently on devices with fingerprint overlapped on power button, behavior of the device can be unpredictable when the user presses powerbutton with an enrolled finger when on lock screen. The behavior depends on the order in which powerd and biod sees the events. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Order of events as seen by | Current behavior | Expected behavior | biod and powerd | | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ PWRBTN DOWN, PWRBTN UP | Screen turns off | Screen turns off. | FP MATCH | an back on. | Locked. | Initial state: screen on | Unlocked. | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ PWRBTN DOWN, FP MATCH | Screen turns off | Screen turns off. | PWRBTN UP | Unlocked. | Locked. | Initial state: screen on | | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ PWRBTN DOWN, FP MATCH | Screen turns on | Screen turns on. | PWRBTN UP | Unlocked. | Locked. | Initial state: screen off | | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ FP MATCH, PWRBTN DOWN, | Screen turns off | Screen turns off. | FP MATCH | Unlocked. | Locked. | | | | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ This is a fix to address the first 3 scenarios. In this CL, we listen for power button down/up events from powerd. If we see these events in last |kAuthIgnoreTimeoutmsecs|, we assume that fp match is an side effect of user interacting with the power button. Thus we ignore the match. vm_tools: concierge: do not keep xattrs/fflags in VM exports When exporting VMs, do not attempt to store extended attributes or "fflags" (chattr-style attributes). The files that are being archived should be normal files, aside from having the "encrypted" chattr flag set, which can't be preserved in an archive anyway. When libarchive adds files with these flags to a PAX-style tar file, it creates extra sections that GNU tar doesn't understand, which results in confusing error messages when extracting the tarball. Disable them to avoid adding the extra sections when using libarchive's "restricted pax" format so that the resulting tar file is cleanly extract-able with GNU tar and other tar implementations. crash: C++ize anomaly detector and have it use the journal Have anomaly_detector use the systemd journal as its log source instead of reading from /var/log/messages. Audit messages have been moved to /var/log/audit/audit.log, and attempts to make anomaly_detector read two files proved complicated: https://crrev.com/c/1630336 It was cleaner to completely rewrite anomaly detector by migrating it to C++ than to try to fit the current unit tests with the journal implementation. This has the added advantage of reducing the dependencies of the unit test and making it much faster since we no longer need to repeatedly call sleep. It's also now understood by the unit test framework as a group of multiple tests instead of one big test. Reading from journal has several advantages, most of which we aren't taking advantage of in this change, but can done in the future. Possible future improvements: * Use sd_journal_add_match and friends to make following the journal more efficient. * Save the journal cursor between boots to avoid missing certain early-boot and shutdown crashes: https://crbug.com/343954#c8 * Leverage structured audit data. Journald actually has all the audit fields we parse from the audit line as structured data. Use these instead of parsing the audit line.
